messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Javier is a 62-year-old married Latino man who has spent most of his adult life as a dancer, and even now his days are organized around rehearsal studios, backstage corridors, and performance spaces where bodies move close to one another without much warning. He came to treatment months after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that he still struggles to describe directly. When he first tried to talk about it, he would stop mid-sentence, press his fingers to his temples, and say that the worst part “doesn’t come in words.” What returns to him most sharply is sound: the violent burst of impact, the scrape of metal, the blare of a horn that seemed not to end. In his memory, those sounds arrive before any image does, as if he is back inside the collision again with no distance from it. He recalls enough to convey that he believed he was about to die, trapped in the car and unable to stop what was happening. Each time he approaches the memory, what rises with it is a wave of shame so strong that he looks down and goes quiet.

In the weeks after the crash, Javier found that he could not bear the feeling of the event coming toward him in fragments. He began trying hard not to think about it at all. If anything reminded him of that day, he would immediately turn his attention elsewhere, switch on the television, pace the apartment, or force himself to focus on practical tasks. At night he stayed up very late, often long after his wife had gone to bed, because sleep felt dangerous. He did not describe nightmares; rather, he dreaded the unguarded state of lying in the dark when the sounds of the collision might come back into his head. On the nights when he felt those memories pressing in, he would deliberately try to blank out. He described it as making himself “leave” for a while, going numb and distant on purpose so that he did not have to feel fully present in his own body.

As time passed, fear, anger, horror, guilt, and shame all remained close to the surface. Javier had come to believe that the crash said something terrible about him, that it had happened because of the kind of person he was. He could not explain this belief logically, but he held it with certainty and with self-contempt. He also felt increasingly exposed in the world. He was certain that bad things could happen suddenly and that he had no real way to stop them. When he entered any building now, whether a small café or a theater lobby, his attention went first to the exits. He mapped the doors before he could settle into where he was. In dance spaces this became especially pronounced. A rehearsal studio that had once felt familiar now registered to him as a place where he needed an escape route. He would note the main door, the side door, the hallway beyond, and only then try to attend to the work.

His work became more difficult in another way as well. Dance had always involved touch—partners placing a hand at his shoulder blade, a choreographer adjusting his arm, another performer brushing past him in the wings. Since the collision, unexpected touch makes him jolt with alarm. Colleagues have noticed him flinch or twist away before recognizing where he is. He feels embarrassed each time it happens, and that embarrassment has added to the shame he already carries. At home, his wife has also become more cautious with him. If she comes up behind him and touches his arm without warning, he startles hard enough that both of them go silent afterward. The strain is not dramatic, but it has changed the atmosphere between them; there is more watching, more hesitating.

Javier also speaks with grief about what he calls his missing feelings. He does not mean that he feels nothing—if anything, painful feelings come too easily—but that ordinary emotions no longer seem available in the way they once were. He has come to believe he will never feel normal again, never fully recover the ease, warmth, or uncomplicated pleasure that used to accompany dancing, teaching, and being with his wife. This conviction has made the future feel narrowed and bleak.

He sought help only after a recent rehearsal in which another dancer touched him unexpectedly from behind to cue an entrance and he recoiled so sharply that the room fell quiet. Later, trying to explain himself, he found again that he could not put the crash into words; instead he heard the sounds in his head and felt that same hot shame. What frightened him most in coming to therapy was the possibility that this damaged, watchful version of himself was permanent. What he hoped for, though he said it tentatively, was to be able to stay present in his own body again, to walk into a room without immediately searching for a way out, and to stand beside his wife without bracing for the next terrible thing.
